title: Capitulation
teaches: The capitulation as we trade it: a straight-down burst in a liquid stock or index, ending in a flush day whose low sits 2 ATR or more under the prior close on at least twice the usual volume, 15% or more off the 10-session high. We never buy the falling price or the flush close. We buy the undercut and reclaim of the flush low within 3 sessions, stop a few cents under the low of the day we bought, take the first sell as a judgment, usually day 3 or later into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, and accept the stop as the cost of being early.

walkthroughs.title: ALB, May 2010: the tiny stop
steps: May 6, 2010, the flash crash. ALB drops 17.2% off its 10-day high close, after three lower closes.
That's the flush. We don't buy that close. We wait for the turn.
May 7 it undercuts 38.31 and closes 39.23. We buy the reclaim at market, 38.49.
Stop 38.26, just 0.6% away. With a stop that tight, 5R is only about 3% above your buy.

walkthroughs.title: OKTA, April 2025: the Monday turn
steps: OKTA, April 2025. Thursday and Friday it flushes 23.4% off its 10-day high close, on 2.28x volume.
Monday, April 7, it opens 88.34, under the flush low. It undercuts to 87.93, then closes 91.24.
Buy the reclaim at market, 89.37. Stop a few cents under the undercut low, 87.88, 1.7% away.
Down days into a Friday, then a Monday gap that gets bought. Bracco calls that the Monday Effect. Learn to spot it.

walkthroughs.title: BN, March 2020: the crash had one more leg
steps: Not every flush is the bottom. BN, March 9, 2020: down 16.5% off its 10-day high on 3.03x volume.
Next day it reclaims. Buy at market, 19.57, stop 19.40. That's only 0.89% of risk.
March 11 the low hits 18.98, right through the stop. The index made a new low that same week.
The crash had one more leg. BN traded 41% under the buy. The stop kept that a tiny loss.

questions.q: A stock's been sliding for days. Then comes the day it finally breaks. What does a real flush day look like on the chart?
choices: A huge, wide red bar on heavy volume
A small red bar that closes on its low
A close just under the lower band
A quiet drift lower on light volume
questions.answer: A huge, wide red bar on heavy volume
questions.why: A huge, wide red bar on heavy volume. That's the day the holders who've been hanging on finally give up all at once. The selling speeds up, the bar gets way wider than a normal day, and volume spikes. You'll see it jump off the chart next to the bars before it. A lot of the time it closes well off its low, because bigger buyers step in and take those shares. The flush isn't the buy, though. It just tells you the panic might be close to done.
questions.lesson_line: A flush jumps off the chart: a wide red bar on huge volume.

wrong.A small red bar that closes on its low: Small is the problem. A flush is the day the selling goes wild, a bar way bigger than the ones before it.
wrong.A close just under the lower band: A close under the lower Bollinger band only shows a stretch. Plenty of slow slides close under it.
wrong.A quiet drift lower on light volume: That's a grind, not a panic. Nobody's giving up on light volume.

questions.simple: A flush day is a huge red bar on heavy volume, the day holders finally give up and sell.

reasons: house: proposed card criterion, owner review is the gate
the 2 ATR threshold is a proposal that may change

deeper.example: A CMT teacher describes a climax the same way. The trend speeds up, the daily spreads get much wider and the decline gets steeper. Volume gets extremely heavy. Wyckoff adds that the climax often closes well off its low, as larger buyers take the shares.

questions.q: After three days of panic selling, a stock closes right on its low. In a capitulation, that close is our buy.
questions.why: False. I never buy the flush close. Nearly half of flush closes get undercut the next day, so buying it is catching the knife. A close on the low tells you the panic's still running. It doesn't tell you it's over. We wait for the turn: price trades under the flush low, then back over it. That's when the sellers are done and buyers show their hand. You'll pay a bit more than the low, and that's fine.
questions.lesson_line: Never buy the flush close. Buy the turn.
questions.simple: False. Nearly half of flush closes get undercut the next day, so we wait for the turn instead.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: The daily trigger is the undercut and ___ of the flush low.
questions.why: Reclaim. Our card's daily trigger is the undercut and reclaim. Within 3 sessions after the flush day, a session trades below the flush low and then back above it. We buy at the reclaim of the flush low. The dip under the low is not the buy on its own.
questions.lesson_line: Undercut, then reclaim. The reclaim is the buy.
questions.simple: The word is reclaim, because we buy when price climbs back above the flush low after dipping under it.

reasons: the daily trigger and its 3-session window are pending D-003

questions.q: Days of selling, then today prints the biggest volume bar on the whole chart, right at the lows. What's that volume telling you?
choices: Fear's in, holders are giving up
Sellers are only getting started
The selling is calm and orderly
A new uptrend starts right here
questions.answer: Fear's in, holders are giving up
questions.why: Fear's in, and holders are giving up. That's what huge volume at the lows means. People who swore they'd hold are dumping shares at any price. Somebody bigger is on the other side taking them, and that's how a bottom gets built. It's not the buy yet, though. A climax still has to be tested and hold before it's more than a short-term flush. So mark the low and watch what price does with it next.
questions.lesson_line: Huge volume at the lows is panic, not control.

wrong.The selling is calm and orderly: Calm selling comes on light volume. The biggest bar on the chart is panic.
wrong.Sellers are only getting started: It's the end of the selling, not the start. The biggest bar at the lows is the crowd capitulating.
wrong.A new uptrend starts right here: Too early. The flush has to be tested and hold first, and plenty of them make one more low.

questions.simple: Fear has set in. Holders are giving up and dumping shares, and bigger buyers are taking them.

reasons: three publishers agree (Kell on TraderLion, Wyckoff on StockCharts, a CMT teacher on IBKR Campus)
the TraderLion archive capture and the IBKR Campus page were unreachable to WebFetch on 2026-11-12; the Wyckoff quote was re-found

deeper.counter: Oliver Kell reads heavy volume at the lows the same way: fear has set in and traders are capitulating. The Wyckoff school calls it a selling climax, panicky selling by the public taken by larger interests near a bottom.

questions.q: A stock grinds lower for three weeks, and its volume gets lighter every week. That's a capitulation.
questions.why: False. Nobody's panicking there. A capitulation is the moment holders give up all at once. That shows up as heavy volume on a fast, wide drop. Lighter volume every week means sellers are just leaking out. The stock can still bottom that way, because some downtrends end quietly with no climax at all. It's just not this trade. There's no flush low for you to undercut, reclaim and stop out under.
questions.lesson_line: No panic on the volume, no capitulation.
questions.simple: False. Lighter volume means no panic, and a capitulation is the day holders give up all at once.

questions.q: How much volume do we want on the flush day?
choices: At least twice the 50-day average
About 1.5 times the 50-day average
About the 50-day average volume
Any volume will do on a big drop
questions.why: At least 2 times the 50-day average. That is the floor. Ideally the flush day is the highest volume of the decline or of the year. Climaxes bring extremely heavy volume, so ordinary volume does not mark one. A decline on falling volume does not qualify at all.
questions.lesson_line: A flush needs at least twice the usual volume.

wrong.About the 50-day average volume: Ordinary volume does not mark a flush. We want at least 2 times.
wrong.Any volume will do on a big drop: Volume is one of the gates. A decline on falling volume does not qualify.
wrong.About 1.5 times the 50-day average: That falls short. The card's floor is at least 2 times the 50-day average.

questions.simple: At least twice the 50-day average, because a real panic shows up as very heavy volume.

reasons: the 2x volume is the dossier's own proposal and may change

questions.q: Tap the number for a stock, not a 3x ETF.
questions.sentence: A stock must fall at least ___ from its highest close of the last 10 sessions.
questions.why: 15%. Our card asks a stock to fall at least 15% from its highest close of the last 10 sessions. A 3x ETF needs 30% instead. Measure from the highest close, not from the intraday high.
questions.lesson_line: Stocks need 15% off the 10-session high. 3x ETFs need 30%.
questions.simple: A stock must fall at least 15% from its highest close of the last 10 sessions to count.

reasons: the 15% / 30% stretch is the dossier's proposal, waiting on the owner's review

questions.q: How far under its 50-day should an index close in a flush?
choices: At least 3 ATR
At least 2 ATR
At least 1 ATR
At least 15%
questions.why: At least 3 ATR under the 50-day SMA. That is the card's stretch for an index. Bracco finds intermediate corrections typically bottom around an average of 3 ATR below the 50-day. It is a typical zone, not a promise.
questions.lesson_line: An index flush closes 3 ATR or more under its 50-day.

wrong.At least 1 ATR: The card asks for at least 3 ATR under the 50-day. One ATR falls well short.
wrong.At least 2 ATR: 2 ATR is the flush day's drop from the prior close. The index stretch is at least 3 ATR under the 50-day.
wrong.At least 15%: 15% is the stretch for a stock, from its 10-day high close. An index is measured in ATR.

questions.simple: At least 3 ATR under its 50-day, because intermediate corrections tend to bottom around there.

questions.q: After a real capitulation flush, price sits under its 9 and 20 EMA.
questions.why: True. A flush is fast and violent, so it slices right through the short averages. If price is still holding its 20 EMA, you're looking at a pullback in a healthy trend, not a panic. Being under them isn't the buy, though. It just tells you how stretched the stock is. The buy still comes on the turn, when price reclaims the flush low.
questions.lesson_line: A real flush cuts through the short averages.
questions.simple: True. A flush is fast, so price falls right through the 9 and 20 EMA on the way down.

reasons: a proposed card criterion, waiting on the owner's review

questions.q: How many lower closes should come before the flush day?
choices: At least 2
None; a one-day shock counts
At least 10
Exactly 1
questions.why: At least 2. A capitulation is not a one-day shock out of nowhere. It comes after the stock has already been falling.
questions.lesson_line: Two or more lower closes come before the flush.

wrong.None; a one-day shock counts: A one-day shock out of nowhere is not the setup.
wrong.At least 10: The burst is a few days, not ten.
wrong.Exactly 1: One lower close is not enough. We want at least 2.

questions.q: A stock closes under its lower Bollinger band after a hard drop. That close is a buy signal.
questions.why: False. That close only tells you the stock is stretched. It's not a turn. Closes outside the bands are at first continuation signals, so a stock can walk down the lower band for days. I use it as a bit of extra evidence that the selling's gone too far. The buy is still the reclaim of the flush low, where you can put a tight stop right under the turn.
questions.lesson_line: A band close is evidence. The reclaim is the trigger.
questions.simple: False. A close under the lower band shows a stretch, not a turn, and the stock can keep falling.

deeper.counter: John Bollinger says it himself: a tag of the lower band is not in and of itself a buy signal. Closes outside the bands are at first continuation signals, not reversal signals.

questions.q: You want in on the bounce. What has to happen before you buy?
choices: Trade under this low, then back over
Nothing, buy this flush day's close
A break over the flush day's high
Any green day after the flush
questions.answer: Trade under this low, then back over
questions.why: It has to trade under this low and then back over it. That's the undercut and reclaim, and you buy the reclaim at market as price comes back through the flush low. The wait is worth it. The undercut shakes out the last weak holders, and the reclaim shows buyers stepped in. You also get a tight stop, a few cents under that day's low. This one did it the next day. It hit 3R on day 1 and was up 88% inside 60 sessions.
questions.lesson_line: Undercut the flush low, reclaim it, buy it.

wrong.Nothing, buy this flush day's close: That's catching the knife. Nearly half of flush closes get undercut the next day.
wrong.A break over the flush day's high: That's paying way up for the same turn, with your stop miles away under the low.
wrong.Any green day after the flush: A green day can still be a dead bounce. It needs to take out the low and reclaim it.

questions.simple: Wait for price to dip under the flush low and climb back over it. That reclaim is the buy.

reasons: the daily trigger and its 3-session window are pending D-003

questions.story: The last bar is the flush day. A leader just fell 21% in two sessions, down to the top of its old base and its rising 50-day.

questions.q: Before a capitulation is a trade for us, the stock has to be $10 or more and trade $20 million a day.
questions.why: True. Same liquidity line as every trade we take. Panic is exactly when thin stocks get ugly. Spreads blow out, your stop can fill way under where you set it, and getting out costs you. A $10 stock trading $20 million a day lets you get in and out clean, even on the worst day. A cheap or thin name isn't for us, however good the flush looks.
questions.lesson_line: $10 or more, $20 million a day. Even in a panic.
questions.simple: True. We only trade stocks at $10 or more that trade $20 million a day, so we can get out clean.

questions.q: Lots of lines on this chart. Which level makes this flush worth watching?
choices: The 100 area and the 200-day
A minor low from last week
The 9 EMA, just above price
The lower Bollinger band
questions.why: The 100 area and the 200-day. Those are levels the whole market watches. Big buyers have orders sitting there, and that's where a panic can finally run into real demand. A flush into a random spot has nothing to catch it. So when a straight-down fall lands on a big round number and the 200-day, I'm paying attention. The next day it undercut the low and closed 6% higher. That reclaim was the buy.
questions.lesson_line: Location matters. Look for a flush into a level everyone watches.

wrong.A minor low from last week: Nobody's waiting at last week's minor low. It doesn't carry the weight to stop a panic.
wrong.The lower Bollinger band: The lower band moves with price. It shows a stretch, not a level where buyers are waiting.
wrong.The 9 EMA, just above price: The flush fell through the 9 EMA. It's above price now, so it isn't catching anything.

questions.simple: The 100 area and the 200-day. Big buyers wait at levels like that, so a panic can stop there.
questions.story: The last bar is the flush day. Three lower closes in a row, and the fall ran straight down into the round number 100 and the 200-day.

questions.q: Prior close 80.00, ATR 2.50, today's low 74.60. How many ATR under the prior close is the low?
questions.why: 2.16 ATR. Take the drop, 80.00 minus 74.60, and divide it by the ATR of 2.50. That gives 2.16. Our card wants the flush day's low at least 2 ATR under the prior close, so this clears the bar.
questions.lesson_line: Drop in dollars, divided by the ATR.
questions.simple: The low is 2.16 ATR under the prior close, because the dollar drop divided by the 2.50 ATR gives 2.16.

reasons: the 2 ATR flush line is a proposed card criterion

choices: 5.40 ATR
0.46 ATR
6.75 ATR
2.16 ATR

wrong.5.40 ATR: Gave the dollar drop and skipped the ATR division.
wrong.0.46 ATR: Flipped the division, ATR over the drop.
wrong.6.75 ATR: Used the percent drop as ATR.

questions.q: The highest close of the last 10 sessions was 120.00 and the flush low is 100.00. How far is the drop, in percent?
questions.why: 16.7%. Take the drop, 120.00 minus 100.00, and divide it by the high close of 120.00. That gives 16.7%. A stock needs at least 15% off its highest close of the last 10 sessions, so this one clears the stretch.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the drop from the 10-session high close.
questions.simple: The drop is 16.7% from the 120.00 high close, and that clears the 15% a stock needs.

reasons: the 15% stretch is the dossier's proposal

wrong.20.0%: Divided by the flush low, not the high close.
wrong.83.3%: Gave the low as a share of the high.
wrong.1.7%: Slipped the decimal point a place.

questions.q: QQQ's 50-day is 500 and its ATR is 8. After a week of selling it closes at 472. How many ATR under the 50-day is it?
questions.why: 3.5 ATR. 500 minus 472 is 28 points, and 28 divided by the 8 point ATR is 3.5. Measuring in ATR tells you how stretched the index is against its own normal daily move. Bracco has found that intermediate corrections find a tradable bottom around 3 ATR under the 50-day, on average. So QQQ is in the zone where I start watching for a turn. That's a heads-up, not a buy. The buy still needs a reclaim.
questions.lesson_line: Measure an index stretch in ATR under its 50-day.
questions.simple: QQQ sits 3.5 ATR under its 50-day, the kind of stretch where index corrections have found a bottom.

reasons: the 3 ATR index stretch is a proposed card criterion

choices: 28.0 ATR
0.3 ATR
3.5 ATR
5.6 ATR

wrong.28.0 ATR: That's the gap in points. Divide it by the 8 point ATR to get 3.5.
wrong.0.3 ATR: Flipped it. That's the ATR over the gap, 8 over 28.
wrong.5.6 ATR: That's the gap as a percent, 28 over 500. We want it in ATR, so divide by 8.

questions.q: A Wyckoff trader buys right into the selling climax, at the day's low.
questions.why: False. Even the Wyckoff school waits. The climax is where panicky selling gets soaked up by bigger players, but the buy is the test after it. A spring or a shakeout that holds is the high-probability trade. It's the same thing we do. The flush tells you the panic may be done. The undercut and reclaim proves it, and it gives you a low to stop out under.
questions.lesson_line: Even the Wyckoff school waits for the test.
questions.simple: False. The Wyckoff trader waits for a test of the low, like a spring, before buying.

reasons: two publishers agree (StockCharts Wyckoff tutorial, CMT on IBKR Campus)
the IBKR Campus page answered 403 to WebFetch on 2026-11-12; the Wyckoff quote was re-found

questions.q: Kell says trading the daily Reversal Extension at once is often best avoided.
questions.why: True. Kell says trading the daily Reversal Extension is often best avoided. We do not buy the falling price either.
questions.lesson_line: The early buy is the risky buy.

questions.q: In Bracco's studies, notable capitulations and turns have come on a Monday.
questions.why: True. That's from his own studies of past washouts. Several down days into a Friday, then Monday gaps down and the selling finally runs out. OKTA's a good one. It flushed into a Friday, then Monday opened under the flush low and closed above it. Treat it as a heads-up, not a rule. A Monday doesn't make the trade. The reclaim does.
questions.lesson_line: Down into Friday, flush Monday. Watch for the turn.
questions.simple: True. Bracco found notable turns come on a Monday, after a run of down days into a Friday.

reasons: Bracco's Monday list has a typo the dossier flags (D-015); no date is keyed

questions.q: A capitulation long needs an RS rating of 80 or more before we'll take it.
questions.why: False. For breakouts we want leaders, RS 80 or more in a strong group. Mean-reversion trades like this one are exempt. Right after a flush, a stock's RS has just been beaten up, so the rating can't tell you much. You're trading the panic and the turn, not the trend. I'd still rather take it in a real leader that got hit, though. Bracco uses this long to get exposure to powerful, trending leaders.
questions.lesson_line: No RS bar here, but a leader that flushed is still the best one.
questions.simple: False. Mean-reversion trades skip the RS 80 rule, though a beaten-up leader is still the one I want.

questions.q: Do you buy this close, or wait?
choices: Wait for the undercut and reclaim
Buy the close, the low is in
Wait a week for it to settle
Buy tomorrow's open no matter what
questions.story: The last bar is the flush day. Three lower closes in a row, and today closes right on its low. Everyone on your feed is calling the bottom.
questions.answer: Wait for the undercut and reclaim
questions.why: Wait. A close right on the low means sellers were still hitting it into the bell. That's the panic, not the end of it. Nearly half of flush closes get undercut the next day. So I let the next session show me. If it trades under this low and climbs back over it, that's my buy. The stop goes a few cents under the new low. This one did exactly that: the next session undercut it and closed 6% higher.
questions.lesson_line: Buy the turn, not the knife.

wrong.Wait a week for it to settle: By then the turn has often come and gone. This one turned the very next session.
wrong.Buy the close, the low is in: A close on the low shows the panic. It doesn't show the low is in.
wrong.Buy tomorrow's open no matter what: A blind open can sit under the low and keep falling. Wait for the reclaim.

questions.simple: Wait. The flush close is often not the low, so buy only when price breaks it and climbs back.

deeper.trap: A close right on the low tempts you to buy the bottom. It means the opposite: sellers were still pressing at the bell. Let the next day undercut it and reclaim it, and buy that, with the stop under the new low.

reasons: keys the daily trigger, pending D-003

questions.q: Where exactly do you get in?
choices: As it climbs back over the flush low
At 59.63, the new low of the day
At the close of the flush day
On a break of the flush day's high
questions.story: The last bar is the flush day. The next morning price trades down to 59.63, under the flush low, then climbs back over it and closes at 61.82.
questions.answer: As it climbs back over the flush low
questions.why: As it climbs back over the flush low, at market. The dip to 59.63 is the undercut, the last sellers getting shaken out. The reclaim is buyers taking it back. Your stop goes a few cents under 59.63, the low of the day you bought. That keeps the risk small, because the low is right there. If it breaks that low again, the turn failed and you're out small.
questions.lesson_line: Undercut the flush low, then buy the reclaim.

wrong.At the close of the flush day: That's the knife. Nearly half of flush closes get undercut the next day, like this one was.
wrong.At 59.63, the new low of the day: That's buying while it's still falling. You don't know it's the low until it reclaims.
wrong.On a break of the flush day's high: That's paying up for the same turn, with the stop much farther away.

questions.simple: Buy at market as price climbs back over the flush low, with the stop under that day's low.

reasons: the daily trigger is pending D-003 and the setup's stop D-008; keyed on the settled house stop

questions.q: How far is that stop from your buy, in percent?
questions.why: 0.6%. 38.49 minus 38.26 is 0.23 a share, and 0.23 over 38.49 is 0.6%. That's tiny, tighter than even the 1-3% we like. The stop sits a few cents under 38.31, the low of the day you bought, because that's where the turn fails. A stop that tight keeps your dollar risk small. Just don't let it talk you into a monster position, because a stop can't catch an overnight gap.
questions.lesson_line: Stop a few cents under the low you bought. Then do the math.
questions.simple: The stop is 0.6% away, because it sits just under the low of the day you bought.

deeper.example: ALB, May 2010: with a stop 0.6% under the buy, 5R was only about 3% above it. The bounce didn't need to be big to pay. The same tightness means a normal wiggle can take you out, so accept that before you buy.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A3, F62) and an example the owner has not reviewed (D-007); stop width is D-041

wrong.6.0%: Slipped the decimal. 0.23 over 38.49 is 0.6%, not 6%.
wrong.23.0%: That reads the 23 cents as a percent. Divide it by the 38.49 buy.
wrong.3.0%: That's a normal stop width, not this one. Run the real numbers.

questions.story: This is the reclaim day. You bought at 38.49 as price came back over the flush low. The undercut low was 38.31, so your stop's at 38.26.

questions.q: Where's 5R on this trade?
questions.why: 39.64. One R is your risk per share: 38.49 minus 38.26 is 0.23. Five of those is 1.15. Add that to the 38.49 buy and 5R sits at 39.64. That's only about 3% over your buy. With a stop this tight, the R marks come fast. 5R is a mark to measure the trade by, not an order to sell. Selling into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, or at about 5 to 10R, is often best.
questions.lesson_line: R is your risk per share. 5R is five of them over your buy.
questions.simple: 5R is 39.64: five times the 0.23 risk per share, added to the 38.49 buy.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E51) and the ALB example (D-007)

wrong.38.72: That's 1R. You added one risk unit, not five.
wrong.39.41: You added five R to the stop, not to the buy.
wrong.39.87: That's six R. One too many.

questions.story: You bought the reclaim at 38.49 with the stop at 38.26, a few cents under the low of the day.

questions.q: Is this a capitulation you can trade?
choices: No, it's an earnings reaction
Yes, earnings fear is still panic
Yes, 20% is deep enough
No, it fell too slowly
questions.story: A leader drops 20% in two days, starting the morning after it reports earnings. Volume is huge and the low looks like panic.
questions.why: No. That's an earnings reaction. If it's earnings, it's just earnings. The market is repricing the business on new numbers. That's a different thing from holders panicking out with no news. In a panic flush, sellers dump shares at any price. After a report, buyers and sellers are arguing over what the company's worth now. The size and speed of the drop don't decide it. The report does. Earnings gaps get their own lessons.
questions.lesson_line: If it's earnings, it's just earnings. Keep it apart from a panic.

wrong.Yes, earnings fear is still panic: A bad report isn't panic selling. It's the market repricing the business.
wrong.Yes, 20% is deep enough: Depth isn't the test here. The report behind the drop is what rules it out.
wrong.No, it fell too slowly: Speed isn't the issue. Two days is fast. The report is what makes it a different trade.

questions.simple: No. A drop right after earnings is the market repricing the business, not holders panicking out.

reasons: scan numbers that change with a rescan

deeper.example: When our research scan checked report dates, 150 of 346 above-200-day hits had a report inside the flush window. Those weren't panics at all. They were earnings reactions, and they get traded as earnings.

questions.q: The reclaim triggers in the morning. Do you take it?
choices: No, the report is 2 sessions away
Yes, the reclaim is the trigger
Yes, but at half size to be safe
No, earnings means skip a month
questions.story: The last bar is the day before the reclaim. If it triggers tomorrow, the company reports earnings two sessions later.
questions.answer: No, the report is 2 sessions away
questions.why: No. We take no new buys in the 3 days before an earnings report, and 2 sessions away is inside that. A clean trigger doesn't override it, and half size doesn't either. Here's the reason. A bounce trade lives on a tight stop under the low. A report can gap the stock right through that stop overnight, and a small planned loss turns into a big one. Now it's a bet on the news, not a read of the chart. Pass, and take a fresh look after the report.
questions.lesson_line: A clean trigger still waits out the report.

wrong.Yes, but at half size to be safe: Half size still carries a gap through your stop. No new buy inside the 3 days.
wrong.Yes, the reclaim is the trigger: The trigger's real, but the report window comes first. A gap on the news ignores your stop.
wrong.No, earnings means skip a month: Too long. The window is the 3 days before a report. After it, take a fresh look.

questions.simple: No. A report can gap the stock right through your stop, so we never buy in the 3 days before one.

questions.q: Do you still buy it here?
choices: No, it's 4.8% past the trigger
Yes, the setup is still intact
Yes, with a wider stop to fit it
No, never buy over the trigger
questions.story: The trigger price is 50.00. You got stuck on a call, and by the time you look, the stock trades at 52.40.
questions.why: No. 52.40 minus 50.00 is 2.40, and 2.40 over 50.00 is 4.8% past the trigger. Our line is 4% over the buy point, and this is past it. Chasing costs you size, not risk. Your stop still belongs under the low of the day, so the distance grows and the shares shrink. You'd own a smaller position at a worse price, on a bounce that already moved without you. I'd rather miss it than chase it.
questions.lesson_line: Past 4% over the trigger, let it go.

wrong.Yes, with a wider stop to fit it: A wider stop is just a bigger loss if it fails. The stop stays where the chart puts it.
wrong.Yes, the setup is still intact: An intact setup still has a chase limit. Past 4%, you're paying for someone else's entry.
wrong.No, never buy over the trigger: Too strict. Up to 4% over the trigger is fine. This one is 4.8%.

questions.simple: No. 52.40 is 4.8% past the 50.00 trigger, over our 4% chase line, so let it go.

deeper.counter: Half size or a wider stop feels like a fix for a late look. It isn't. The stop stays under the low, so a higher buy only adds distance and cuts the shares. Past 4% over the trigger, it's a pass. Wait for a new trigger.

questions.q: Is that close your trigger?
choices: No, it's a stretch, not a trigger
Yes, a close outside is the trigger
Yes, after a third close outside
No, the bands never matter
questions.story: A stock in a hard drop closes under its lower Bollinger band for the second day in a row. A friend texts you that it's a screaming buy.
questions.answer: No, it's a stretch, not a trigger
questions.why: No. Two closes under the lower band tell you the stock is stretched, and that's all. Closes outside the bands are at first continuation signals, so a falling stock can ride the lower band for a week. A second close outside isn't more proof of a bottom. It's proof the selling's still on. I'll note the stretch, then wait for the flush low to get undercut and reclaimed. That's a real turn, with a low to put your stop under.
questions.lesson_line: A stretched close is not a turn.

wrong.Yes, a close outside is the trigger: A band tag isn't a buy signal by itself. Price can keep walking down the lower band.
wrong.Yes, after a third close outside: More closes outside mean the trend is still running, not ending.
wrong.No, the bands never matter: They help as a read on the stretch. They just don't tell you when to buy.

questions.simple: No. Closing under the lower band shows a stretch, and it can keep falling, so wait for the turn.

deeper.trap: A second close under the band feels like more proof of a bottom. John Bollinger reads it the other way: closes outside the bands are at first continuation signals. Use the band as evidence of a stretch, and wait for the turn.

questions.q: What's that day telling you?
choices: A warning, but the stop decides
A gift, add more on the dip
Nothing, it's only one candle
Lower the stop to give it room
questions.story: You bought the reclaim at 92.82. The next day opens higher at 93.75, then sells off all day and closes in the lower tenth of its range.
questions.answer: A warning, but the stop decides
questions.why: It's a warning, but your stop decides. A real turn should have buyers pushing on day 1. Opening up and closing near the low says sellers took it right back. That's the early sign the bounce is weak. It doesn't move your stop, and it doesn't change your size. This one went from a 93.75 open to an 87.89 close, right through the stop. The stop did its job and kept the loss small. Never lower it, and never average down.
questions.lesson_line: A weak first bounce is a warning. The stop stays put.

wrong.A gift, add more on the dip: We never average down. Full size once, at one price, with one stop.
wrong.Nothing, it's only one candle: A first-day stall is the early warning on these. Respect it.
wrong.Lower the stop to give it room: The stop only moves up, never down. Lowering it just makes the loss bigger.

questions.simple: It's a warning that the bounce is weak, but the stop still decides when you're out.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4) and a proposed card criterion

questions.q: Big drop, big volume. Is this a capitulation?
choices: No, there was no burst before it
Yes, the flush day is big enough
Yes, three weeks down is the burst
No, the drop isn't deep enough
questions.story: The last bar is the flush day. Before it, three weeks of choppy, controlled selling. Today it drops 2.61 ATR on 2.02 times its usual volume, 15.3% off its 10-day high.
questions.answer: No, there was no burst before it
questions.why: No. Look left before you look at the last bar. Three weeks of choppy, controlled selling isn't a panic. Nobody was rushing for the exits. A capitulation comes at the end of a burst, days of faster and faster selling where holders finally break. One big day after a slow grind is a controlled mark down with a bad day in it. Bracco calls that out too: no fear, no panic, just a choppy, controlled mark down. That's not a setup.
questions.lesson_line: Look left. A slow grind is not a burst.

wrong.Yes, the flush day is big enough: The last day is big, but one day isn't the setup. What came before matters.
wrong.Yes, three weeks down is the burst: Three weeks of chop is a grind. A burst is days of fast, speeding-up selling.
wrong.No, the drop isn't deep enough: Depth isn't the problem. 15.3% off the high is a real drop. The missing burst is.

questions.simple: No. The stock slid slowly for weeks, and a slow grind isn't the fast burst of panic we want.

deeper.example: MS is the case: the last day was 2.61 ATR on 2.02 times volume, 15.3% off the 10-day high, into the 200-day. It looked the part. But it came at the end of a controlled three-week mark down, not a burst. No burst, no capitulation.

reasons: the burst idea is held under D-002

questions.q: Capitulation, or not?
choices: No, nothing was falling before it
Yes, a 20% day is a flush
Yes, the heavy volume says panic
No, a 20% fall is too shallow
questions.story: A stock closes flat or higher every day for a week. Then, out of nowhere, it falls 20% in a single session on heavy volume.
questions.answer: No, nothing was falling before it
questions.why: No. There was no fall before it. A capitulation is the end of a run of selling, the day the last holders finally give up. This stock was calm all week, then dropped 20% in one shot. That's a shock, and something caused it, so find out what. A one-day collapse out of a quiet tape is news getting priced in, not tired sellers running out. Bracco has passed on a bounce try that was only the second day down.
questions.lesson_line: No fall before it, no capitulation. A one-day shock is news.

wrong.Yes, a 20% day is a flush: Size alone doesn't make it a flush. There was no run of selling to exhaust.
wrong.Yes, the heavy volume says panic: Heavy volume on a shock day is news being priced in. It's not the end of a panic.
wrong.No, a 20% fall is too shallow: Depth isn't the problem. 20% in a day is huge. What's missing is the fall before it.

questions.simple: No. A capitulation ends a run of selling, and this stock was calm until one shock day.

questions.q: Does the volume qualify?
choices: No; the flush needs 2 times the average
Yes; volume is up
Yes; three down days is enough
No; it must be 10 times
questions.story: A leader is down three days in a row. The flush day trades only 1.3 times its 50-day average volume.
questions.answer: No; the flush needs 2 times the average
questions.why: No. Flush-day volume needs to be at least 2 times the 50-day average, and ideally the highest of the decline.
questions.lesson_line: Modest volume is a pullback, not a panic.

wrong.Yes; volume is up: Up a little is not a panic. The bar is 2 times.
wrong.Yes; three down days is enough: Down days are one gate. Volume is another.

questions.q: Does it pass?
choices: No; volume is just under the 2x bar
Yes; 1.96 rounds up to the 2x bar
Yes; volume is optional on a big ATR
No; the ATR is too small to count
questions.story: The flush day: 2.13 ATR, 15.2% off the 10-day high, above the 200-day. Volume is 1.96 times the 50-day average.
questions.answer: No; volume is just under the 2x bar
questions.why: No. Our card asks flush-day volume of at least 2 times the 50-day average, and 1.96 is under it. The rest of the shape is there: 2.13 ATR and 15.2% off the high. A near miss is still a miss. The 2 times line is the card's proposal, and the test is the number as written.
questions.lesson_line: A near miss is still a miss.

wrong.Yes; 1.96 rounds up to the 2x bar: The test is the number, not a rounding. 1.96 is under 2.
wrong.Yes; volume is optional on a big ATR: Volume is a gate. A big ATR does not stand in for it.

questions.simple: It fails, because 1.96 times the average volume is under the 2 times bar, and a rule is a line.

deeper.trap: The trap is rounding. 1.96 looks like 2, and every other part of the shape is there: 2.13 ATR and 15.2% off the high. But the volume bar is a line, and 1.96 sits under it. Round one gate today and you will round the next one tomorrow.

reasons: the 2x volume bar is the dossier's proposal, and the LLY near miss is from the owner-unreviewed dossier (D-007)

questions.q: It flushed hard and could reclaim tomorrow. What stops the buy?
choices: Price is way under the 200-day
The fall off the high is too small
The flush day wasn't wide enough
Volume wasn't heavy enough
questions.story: The last bar is the day before the reclaim. The stock slid for two months, then flushed 17.6% off its high on 3.48 times its usual volume. Even a reclaim would close 15.9% under its 200-day.
questions.why: Price is way under the 200-day, and that's a hard no for stocks. The flush itself looks real: 17.6% off the high on 3.48 times volume. Doesn't matter. Under the 200-day the bigger money is selling rallies, not buying them, so a bounce runs straight into that supply. Indexes and levered ETFs are the one exception, on a reversal extension or a parabolic long. A single stock never is. Pass, and keep it on your radar for when it's back over the line.
questions.lesson_line: Under the 200-day, no stock longs. Not even a clean flush.

wrong.The fall off the high is too small: 17.6% off the high is plenty. The fall isn't what stops it.
wrong.The flush day wasn't wide enough: The flush was a big, wide day. That isn't the problem.
wrong.Volume wasn't heavy enough: 3.48 times normal is heavy volume. That isn't what stops it.

questions.simple: Price is way under the 200-day, and we don't buy stocks under the 200-day. Pass.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B26); what counts as a parabolic long is held (D-002, D-009, D-119)

questions.q: Bulkowski found that nearly half of one-day collapses make a lower low the next day.
questions.why: True. Bulkowski found that forty-six percent of his one-day collapse events make a lower low the next day. Then 17% continue lower the day after, then 9%, then 3%. So buying the first close is often early. That is why we wait for the turn instead of buying the knife.
questions.lesson_line: Nearly half make a lower low the next day.
questions.simple: True. In his study, nearly half made a lower low the next day, so buying the first close is often early.

reasons: rests on Bulkowski, whose site asks not to be used for AI training (source policy open)

questions.q: After a big one-day drop, Bulkowski's average bounce is how big, and how long?
choices: 28% over 23 days
5% over 2 days
60% over 6 months
No bounce at all
questions.why: 28% over 23 days. That is Bulkowski's average bounce, from the event low to the bounce high, after a one-day collapse. It does not last: price then resumes declining, averaging 30% from the bounce high in 49 days. So the bounce is a trade, not a new trend. Bracco also treats his mean reversion bounces as short lived trades.
questions.lesson_line: The bounce is a trade, not a new trend.

wrong.5% over 2 days: That is far smaller and faster than his average. It is 28% over 23 days.
wrong.60% over 6 months: Too big and too long. The bounce averages 28% in 23 days, then price falls again.
wrong.No bounce at all: There is a bounce. Then price resumes declining, about 30% in 49 days.

questions.simple: His average bounce is 28% over 23 days, and then price tends to fall again.

reasons: rests on Bulkowski, whose site asks not to be used for AI training (source policy open)

questions.q: In Bulkowski's own trades, what share of buys in stage 4, the downtrend, made money?
questions.why: 24.41%. In Bulkowski's own trades, just 24.41% of the stocks bought in stage 4, the downtrend, made money. In stage 1, 69.3% did. It is one trader's record, not a market-wide study. It fits our rule against longs under the 200-day.
questions.lesson_line: Buying a downtrend loses most of the time.

wrong.69.3%: That is the share of stage 1 buys that made money.
wrong.75.59%: That is about the share of stage 4 buys that did not make money.

questions.simple: Only 24.41% of his stage 4 buys made money, far fewer than the 69.3% in stage 1.

reasons: rests on one publisher (Bulkowski); the quote was re-found on 2026-11-12; his site carries a notice against AI training (owner flag)

questions.q: Buy the huge volume now?
choices: Wait; the low broke the next day
Buy now; the volume is huge
Buy half now
Buy the next open
questions.story: A stock falls 77% in 3 days on 7.0x volume. Bracco says a long may set up in the next 1-2 weeks.
questions.answer: Wait; the low broke the next day
questions.why: Wait. Bracco said 1-2 weeks, and the low broke the next day. The stock traded 25% under it within 5 sessions.
questions.lesson_line: Even a 77% fall can fall further. Wait for the turn.

wrong.Buy now; the volume is huge: Huge volume showed the panic. It did not show the low.
wrong.Buy half now: Half a knife is still a knife.
wrong.Buy the next open: The next day broke the low.

questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Get out, 19.30 is 3.5R down
Set the stop at 19.30 and hold
Hold, it should bounce back soon
Add at 19.30 to average down
questions.story: You bought at 20.00 with a stop at 19.80. Overnight news hits. It opens at 19.70, already under your stop, and the first 30-minute low is 19.30.
questions.why: Get out. On a gap through your stop, the first 30 minutes decide. The low of that first 30-minute bar becomes your new stop, with one ceiling: past 2R, you're out. Your R here is 20.00 minus 19.80, so 0.20. At the 30-minute low you're 20.00 minus 19.30, so 0.70 down. 0.70 over 0.20 is 3.5R. That's well past 2R, so you sell. You can't stop a gap. You can keep it from getting worse.
questions.lesson_line: A gap through the stop gets 30 minutes. Past 2R, you're out.

wrong.Add at 19.30 to average down: Never average down. One price, one stop.
wrong.Set the stop at 19.30 and hold: That's the gap rule without its ceiling. Past 2R in the first 30 minutes, you're out.
wrong.Hold, it should bounce back soon: Hope isn't a plan. The ceiling is there so one gap can't wreck your month.

questions.simple: Get out. The first 30 minutes took the loss to 3.5R, past the 2R line, so you sell.

deeper.trap: The gap rule lets the stop move to the first 30-minute low. It doesn't let the loss grow without a limit. Here that low is 3.5R under the buy, past the 2R ceiling, so you're out. Hoping for a bounce is the exact move the ceiling exists to stop.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B20 and its 2R ceiling)

questions.q: What do you do at the open?
choices: Weigh selling some into the gap
Sell a third, the gap forces it
Hold it all, never sell this early
Add more at 26.00 on the gap
questions.story: You bought the reclaim at 22.13 with the stop at 21.72. 5R is 24.18. The next morning it gaps up and opens at 26.00.
questions.answer: Weigh selling some into the gap
questions.why: Weigh selling some into the gap. It's a judgment, not a rule. I very rarely sell on day 1, and day 3 is the earliest I'd normally look. But 26.00 is far past the 5R line at 24.18, overnight, on a bounce trade. Panic bounces can fade fast. Taking some off into that kind of gift is fair. This one shows why: it opened at 26.00, sold off right through your 21.72 stop and closed at 21.94. Hold it all with no plan and the whole gain can vanish by the close.
questions.lesson_line: A big gap is a time to weigh a sale. Your call, never a rule.

wrong.Add more at 26.00 on the gap: Never add into a gap like this. It's where you weigh selling.
wrong.Sell a third, the gap forces it: No gap forces a sale. Selling part into a big gap is a judgment, never a rule.
wrong.Hold it all, never sell this early: Never is too strong. An early sell is rare, not banned, and this one gave it all back.

questions.simple: Weigh selling some into the gap. The first sell is your call, and a gap never forces it.

deeper.trap: The open looked like a huge win: 26.00 against a 5R line of 24.18. Then MP sold off through its 21.72 stop and closed at 21.94. A big gap on day 1 is a fair time to weigh a part sale. It's your call, not a rule.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F63) and the MP example from the owner-unreviewed dossier (D-007)

questions.q: What decides when you make your first sell?
choices: Judgment, often into a 3 to 7 day push
A fixed third of the shares at 3R
Judgment, best made on the buy day
A fixed half of the shares at 5R
questions.answer: Judgment, often into a 3 to 7 day push
questions.why: Judgment. There's no fixed third at 3R. I very rarely sell on day 1, and day 3 is the earliest I'd normally look. Selling into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, or at about 5 to 10R, is often best. It depends on how the stock acts, how the market's doing and how stretched it gets. This one took until day 3 just to reach 3R. Selling a fixed third right there would be a rule talking, not the chart.
questions.lesson_line: The first sell is a judgment, often into a 3 to 7 day push.

wrong.A fixed third of the shares at 3R: That was an old rule. The first sell is a judgment now, not a fixed spot.
wrong.A fixed half of the shares at 5R: Nothing's fixed. How much and when is a judgment on how it's acting.
wrong.Judgment, best made on the buy day: Day 1 is the day I very rarely sell. Give the push time to happen.

questions.simple: It's a judgment call, often a sale into a push on day 3 or later, not a fixed third at 3R.

reasons: trim at the averages held under D-013

questions.story: You bought the reclaim at 35.06 with the stop at 34.14. It works, but slowly. It reaches 3R on day 3.

questions.q: Once a capitulation bounce works, you can move the stop to breakeven from 2R to 5R, or at your first sell.
questions.why: True. That's our window, from 2R to 5R, or when you make your first sell. Where you land in it is your call. Just know these bounces can fade hard. A fade that comes all the way back to a stop that never moved turns a winner into a loss. Once the stop's at breakeven, a fade costs you the gain, not your money. Don't drag it up so tight that one normal dip takes you out, though.
questions.lesson_line: Breakeven between 2R and 5R, or at the first sell. Bounces fade, so don't sleep on it.
questions.simple: True. Anywhere from 2R to 5R, or at your first sell, because these bounces can fade fast.

reasons: house: proposed card rule inside the B19 window

questions.q: Your capitulation buy dips toward your stop on day 1. Adding here lowers your average and gives the trade a better shot.
questions.why: False. Never average down. You bought full size at one price with one stop, and the stop is where you're wrong. Adding near it doubles down on a trade that's proving you wrong. If the stop hits, you lose twice what you planned. Bracco says it plainly: he never adds when he's down. If it bounces, great, you already own it. If it doesn't, you're out small.
questions.lesson_line: Never average down. One price, one stop.
questions.simple: False. We never add to a loser, because if the stop hits you lose twice what you planned.

questions.q: How do you trail what's left?
choices: A close under the 9 EMA
A trailing stop on the 200-day
A fixed 10% stop under the buy
Sell it all at 5R instead
questions.why: A close under the 9 EMA. That's our trail for a fast mover, and a bounce off a panic low moves fast. The 9 EMA hugs the move, so you stay in while it runs and get out once it rolls over. For a steadier stock you'd give it the 20 EMA. A 200-day trail gives back way too much, and a fixed 10% stop doesn't follow the move at all. This one hit 3R on day 1 and was up 88% inside 60 sessions. That's what the trail is for.
questions.lesson_line: Fast mover, 9 EMA trail. Sell what's left on a close under it.

wrong.A trailing stop on the 200-day: Way too far. You'd hand back most of the bounce before it ever hit.
wrong.A fixed 10% stop under the buy: A fixed stop doesn't follow the move. The 9 EMA does.
wrong.Sell it all at 5R instead: Later sells are a judgment, and the rest gets trailed. Selling it all at 5R caps a big winner.

questions.simple: A close under the 9 EMA. A bounce off a panic low moves fast, and the 9 EMA keeps up with it.

reasons: house: proposed card rule (cap.trail) on the E52 default

questions.story: You bought the reclaim at 18.64 with the stop at 18.27. It runs hard, and you sell some into a push along the way.

questions.q: Bracco treats these as short lived trades, not held longer than 1-3 days.
questions.why: True. Bracco writes that these are short lived trades, not meant to be held longer than 1-3 days. He wrote it about his rubber band longs, a mean reversion play. It is his note, not one of our rules.
questions.lesson_line: Treat the bounce as a short trade, not a new trend.
questions.simple: True. Bracco writes that these bounce trades are short lived, not meant to last more than 1-3 days.

reasons: the time stop is held under D-019
sits beside the house trail of the last third

questions.q: The S&P's been flushing for a week. What backdrop tells you a market-wide washout might be close?
choices: VIX ripping to 30, breadth washed out
VIX ripping to 30, breadth near highs
VIX falling from 30, breadth washed out
VIX calm on a slow drift lower
questions.answer: VIX ripping to 30, breadth washed out
questions.why: VIX ripping toward 30, with breadth washed out. You want real fear, and you want it rising fast. Bracco says a fast VIX move up into 30 is a good time to start watching for a mean reversion trade. Then check breadth. When almost nothing is holding up, the selling has hit everything, and there's not much left to sell. That's when washouts turn. A calm VIX on a slow drift is a controlled mark down, not a panic.
questions.lesson_line: A real washout has fear ripping and breadth crushed.

wrong.VIX falling from 30, breadth washed out: Fear is already fading. You want it rising fast, at the peak of the panic.
wrong.VIX calm on a slow drift lower: No fear, no panic. A slow drift lower is a controlled mark down.
wrong.VIX ripping to 30, breadth near highs: Fear's up, but most stocks are fine. That's a scare, not a washout.

questions.simple: Fear spiking fast, with the VIX toward 30, and breadth washed out. That's when a panic can turn.

questions.q: SPY slices under a big support level it's held for months. What does Bracco say markets like to do at big support?
choices: Undercut it first, then reclaim
Hold it right to the penny
Bounce cleanly just above it
Stall right at it for weeks
questions.why: Undercut it first. Bracco's line is that markets like to undercut big support areas before reclaiming them, if they do. So a break under support isn't automatically the end. It's often the flush that runs the stops sitting under it, and those stops become the fuel. Our trigger works the same way: price goes under the flush low and comes back over it. The reclaim isn't a given, though. Wait for it.
questions.lesson_line: Big support gets undercut before it's reclaimed.

wrong.Hold it right to the penny: Big support rarely holds that cleanly. The stops under it get run first.
wrong.Bounce cleanly just above it: He says markets go under big support first, not bounce right off it.
wrong.Stall right at it for weeks: He describes an undercut and then a reclaim, if it comes. Not weeks of sitting there.

questions.simple: Undercut it first. Big support breaks for a moment, the stops get run, and then price may climb back.

reasons: keys the daily trigger, pending D-003

questions.q: Which setup did you just trade?
choices: Capitulation, the reclaim days later
Parabolic long, same-day VWAP turn
Mean reversion, a dip to the 50-day
Oops reversal, a gap under the low
questions.story: A leader drops 29% in three sessions on huge volume, the biggest bar on the chart. Two sessions after the flush it undercuts the flush low and closes back above it. You buy the reclaim.
questions.why: Capitulation. A panic flush on the biggest volume on the chart. Then the buy came later, when a session undercut the flush low and reclaimed it. That's this setup. A parabolic long is bought the same day, on the intraday turn back over VWAP. You don't wait for another session. Here the reclaim came two sessions later, so it's a capitulation. Both are reclaims, so the word alone won't tell you. Count the sessions.
questions.lesson_line: Same day is a parabolic long. A later reclaim is a capitulation.

wrong.Parabolic long, same-day VWAP turn: A parabolic long is bought that same day on the VWAP reclaim. This came two sessions later.
wrong.Mean reversion, a dip to the 50-day: Nothing here touches the 50-day. A 29% drop on huge volume is a panic, not a dip.
wrong.Oops reversal, a gap under the low: An Oops gaps under the prior day's low in an orderly pullback. This was a crash.

questions.simple: Capitulation. It was bought on an undercut and reclaim sessions after the flush, not the same day.

deeper.trap: Both triggers are a reclaim, so the word alone doesn't tell them apart. Count the sessions. A parabolic long is bought the same day, on the VWAP reclaim. A capitulation waits for a later session to trade under the flush low and back over it. Here that came two sessions later.

reasons: the two triggers are pending D-003 and the setup map D-002 (Capitulation and the Parabolic Long may be one unit)

questions.q: Capitulation, or something milder?
choices: Milder, a leader pulling back
Capitulation, the volume is heavy
Capitulation, it hit the 50-day
Parabolic long, it fell 6% fast
questions.story: A leader drops 6% in one day into its rising 50-day on heavy volume. It's 7% off its 10-day high.
questions.why: Milder. A leader 7% off its high, sitting on its rising 50-day, is a stock pulling back in an uptrend. Nobody's panicking out of it. A capitulation is the end of a straight-down fall, holders giving up after days of selling. One heavy day into a rising line is a different trade, a mean reversion off a level in a leader. Same stock, different plan, different stop. Measure the fall before you name it.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the fall before you name it. 7% is a pullback.

wrong.Capitulation, the volume is heavy: Heavy volume on one day isn't a panic. 7% off the high is a normal pullback.
wrong.Capitulation, it hit the 50-day: Tagging the 50-day is what pullbacks do. It doesn't make it a flush.
wrong.Parabolic long, it fell 6% fast: Our parabolic long needs a burst down, days of speeding-up selling. One 6% day isn't that.

questions.simple: Milder. A leader 7% off its high on its rising 50-day is pulling back, not panicking.

deeper.counter: Heavy volume into the 50-day can feel like panic. Measure it first. 7% off the 10-day high in a leader is a pullback. A one-day drop into a level is a mean-reversion trade with its own rules.

reasons: the 15% stretch and 2x volume are the dossier's proposals

questions.q: What are you looking at here?
choices: An undercut and rally, not a flush
A capitulation, it broke a level
A parabolic long off a fast fall
An Oops reversal, it closed back up
questions.story: A stock in an ordinary pullback opens flat, then dips 1% under a level everyone can see. Its 50-day is still rising and volume is light. It closes back above the level.
questions.answer: An undercut and rally, not a flush
questions.why: An undercut and rally. A small dip under a visible level in a healthy stock, on light volume, and back over it the same day. That's a U&R. A capitulation is a different animal. It needs a straight-down fall that ends in a panic flush on huge volume, and then a reclaim of that flush low. A 1% dip on light volume isn't anybody panicking. Both reclaim a level, so look at what came before the reclaim.
questions.lesson_line: A small dip and a reclaim is a U&R. A flush is a panic.

wrong.A parabolic long off a fast fall: There was no fast fall. It was an ordinary pullback on light volume.
wrong.A capitulation, it broke a level: Breaking a level isn't a flush. There was no fall and no panic volume.
wrong.An Oops reversal, it closed back up: An Oops gaps under the prior day's low. This one opened flat, no gap.

questions.simple: An undercut and rally. A small dip on light volume in a healthy stock isn't a panic flush.

deeper.trap: Both setups undercut a level and close back over it, so the reclaim alone can't tell them apart. Check what came before. A capitulation ends a straight-down panic on huge volume. A U&R comes after an ordinary dip in a stock whose 50-day isn't falling, and it needs no volume.

questions.q: Which setup is this?
choices: An Oops reversal
A capitulation flush
A Wyckoff spring
A parabolic long
questions.story: A stock in an orderly pullback gaps under yesterday's low at the open. It takes that low back the same day, on a narrow range.
questions.why: An Oops reversal. A gap under the prior day's low in a calm, orderly pullback, taken back the same day. A capitulation flush looks nothing like that. It's the end of a straight-down fall, a huge, wide bar on panic volume. A narrow range in an orderly pullback is the opposite. And a spring needs a trading range behind it, which isn't here. Size up the day, and what came before it.
questions.lesson_line: A calm pullback and a narrow range is an Oops, not a flush.

wrong.A Wyckoff spring: A spring dips under the low of a trading range. This stock was pulling back, not ranging.
wrong.A parabolic long: There's no burst down before it. It was an orderly pullback.
wrong.A capitulation flush: A flush is a huge, wide bar at the end of a straight fall. This was a narrow day in a calm pullback.

questions.simple: An Oops reversal. A small gap and reclaim in a calm pullback, not a huge flush at the end of a fall.

deeper.trap: Both an Oops and a capitulation can open under a low and close back over it. Size up the day and what came before. A flush is a wide bar on panic volume at the end of a straight fall. A gap and reclaim on a narrow range in an orderly pullback is an Oops.

questions.q: What are you looking at?
choices: A Wyckoff spring, there's a range
A capitulation, it broke a level
A parabolic long, it broke the floor
An Oops reversal, it closed back in
questions.story: A stock sits in a flat 30-session range. One day it dips 0.5 ATR under the floor, with no gap, and closes back inside the range.
questions.answer: A Wyckoff spring, there's a range
questions.why: A Wyckoff spring. There's a flat range behind the dip, and the stock went under its floor and closed back inside. That's the spring. A capitulation has no range behind it. It's a straight fall that ends in a panic flush. And nothing here gapped, so it isn't an Oops either. When two shapes both dip under a level and come back, look left. What came before tells you which one you've got.
questions.lesson_line: A range behind the dip is a spring. A straight fall is a capitulation.

wrong.A capitulation, it broke a level: A capitulation is a straight fall with no range behind it. This stock was going sideways.
wrong.A parabolic long, it broke the floor: Our parabolic long is a burst down. This stock sat flat and dipped once.
wrong.An Oops reversal, it closed back in: An Oops gaps under the prior day's low in a pullback. This didn't gap, and a flat range isn't a pullback.

questions.simple: A Wyckoff spring. A flat range sits behind the dip, while a capitulation is a straight fall.

deeper.trap: Both shapes dip under a level and close back over it, so the dip alone doesn't tell them apart. Look at what came before. A spring has a flat range behind it. A capitulation has none: it's a straight fall that ends in a panic flush.

reasons: lookalike tells are proposed card rows, pending on their own cards

questions.q: Capitulation, or something else?
choices: A pullback to a rising average
A capitulation low off the EMA
A parabolic long after a drop
An Oops reversal off the EMA
questions.story: A leader drifts lower for six sessions on light volume, with no gaps, down to its rising 20 EMA, and bounces.
questions.answer: A pullback to a rising average
questions.why: A pullback to a rising average. A leader drifting six sessions on light volume and holding its rising 20 EMA is a stock resting in an uptrend. That's the dip you buy in a healthy trend. A capitulation is the opposite: a fast fall that slices through the 9 and 20 EMA on panic volume. Quiet volume and a held average tell you nobody's scared. Same bounce, completely different trade.
questions.lesson_line: A quiet drift to a rising average is a pullback.

wrong.A capitulation low off the EMA: A capitulation falls through the short averages on huge volume. This one held its 20 EMA.
wrong.A parabolic long after a drop: A parabolic long needs a burst down. This was a quiet drift.
wrong.An Oops reversal off the EMA: An Oops gaps under the prior day's low. This stock drifted with no gaps.

questions.simple: A pullback. A quiet drift on light volume to a rising average is a stock resting, not panicking.

deeper.counter: Keep the same rising 20 EMA but change the fall. Say the stock had sliced through the 9 and 20 EMA in a few days. Add panic volume and a huge flush bar. Then you'd be looking at a capitulation. Quiet volume and a held average make it a pullback.

questions.q: Is this a capitulation long?
choices: No, the selling is informed
Yes, the volume is huge
Yes, 40% is a deep flush
No, it fell too far too fast
questions.story: A stock falls 40% in three days after the company admits accounting fraud. Volume is huge.
questions.why: No. The business broke. When a company admits fraud, the sellers aren't panicking. They know something, and they're getting out for a reason. A capitulation is the public dumping shares in fear, with bigger buyers taking the other side. Here the informed money is doing the selling. Huge volume and a 40% fall look the same on a chart, so you have to ask why it fell. I'm not trying to catch that one.
questions.lesson_line: Informed selling is not a capitulation. Ask why it fell.

wrong.Yes, the volume is huge: Huge volume shows selling. It doesn't tell you if it's fear or real news.
wrong.Yes, 40% is a deep flush: Depth isn't the test. The reason for the selling is.
wrong.No, it fell too far too fast: A deep, fast fall doesn't rule it out. The broken business does.

questions.simple: No. The stock fell on real bad news, so the sellers know something, and that isn't panic.

deeper.trap: Fraud news brings the same numbers a flush shows: huge volume and a deep, fast fall. That's why the numbers alone can't clear it. Ask why it fell. When the business itself broke, the selling is informed, not panic, and it's not this setup.

questions.q: What's the index telling you?
choices: Another leg down may be coming
The bounce is likely confirmed
The stop can come off now
It's time to add more shares
questions.story: You bought a leader's reclaim at 19.57 with the stop at 19.40, after a 16.5% flush. The same week, the index breaks to a new low on heavy volume.
questions.answer: Another leg down may be coming
questions.why: Another leg down may be coming. A single stock's bounce needs the market to stop falling. When the index breaks to a new low while you hold, the panic isn't done, and it'll drag your stock with it. Keep the stop where it is and let it do its job. This one was the March 2020 crash. Day 1 traded down to 18.98 and took the stop. The stock then traded 41% under the buy. The stop kept that a small loss.
questions.lesson_line: A new index low while you hold is a warning. Keep the stop.

wrong.The bounce is likely confirmed: A new index low says the opposite. The selling may not be done.
wrong.The stop can come off now: The stop is the exit. It only moves up, never down or off.
wrong.It's time to add more shares: Never average down. One price, one stop.

questions.simple: Another leg down may come. A new low in the index while you hold says the selling isn't done.

deeper.example: BN, March 2020: a 16.5% flush of 3.29 ATR on 3.03 times volume. The reclaim was bought at 19.57 with a stop at 19.40. Day 1 traded to 18.98 and stopped it. The index made a new low that week, and the stock traded 11.55 inside 30 sessions, 41% under the buy. The stop kept the loss small.

reasons: dossier example numbers the owner has not reviewed (D-007)

questions.q: That stings. What do you do now?
choices: Log it, wait for a new trigger
Buy back now, in bigger size
Use a wider stop next time
Call the setup broken
questions.story: You bought the reclaim at 64.66 with the stop at 63.75. The next day trades 23 cents under the stop, takes you out, then closes near its high.
questions.answer: Log it, wait for a new trigger
questions.why: Log it and wait for a new trigger. The stop was right and the trade still lost. That happens. Whipsaws like this are the cost of trading with a tight stop, and it's a cheap cost. Don't buy back out of anger, and don't go bigger to win it back. A new buy needs a new trigger, as a new trade with its own stop. Journal it the same day, so you see the pattern and not just the sting.
questions.lesson_line: A right stop can still lose. Take it, log it, wait for the next trigger.

wrong.Buy back now, in bigger size: Revenge size turns one small loss into a big one. A new buy needs a new trigger.
wrong.Call the setup broken: One planned loss is the cost of the trade, not proof the setup's broken.
wrong.Use a wider stop next time: Widen it to dodge this, and you take bigger losses on every trade that really fails.

questions.simple: Log the loss and wait. A good stop can still lose, and a new buy needs a new trigger.

deeper.example: VOYA, March 2023: the reclaim was bought at 64.66 with a stop at 63.75. Day 1 traded 23 cents under the stop and closed 66.15 near its high. Ten sessions later it was 70.12, 8.4% over the buy. A whipsaw: the stop was right and the trade still lost. The answer is the next trigger, not a wider stop.

reasons: dossier example numbers the owner has not reviewed (D-007)

questions.q: What is the warning sign?
choices: A late reclaim, sector still breaking
The volume was too high
The stop was too wide
The flush was too deep
questions.story: The flush was on a Friday. The reclaim only came on the third session, and the sector is still breaking.
questions.answer: A late reclaim, sector still breaking
questions.why: A late reclaim in a sector still breaking. COP reclaimed on the third session, the next session traded through the stop, and the stop did its job.
questions.lesson_line: A late reclaim in a breaking group is a warning.

wrong.The volume was too high: Heavy volume is wanted in a flush.
wrong.The stop was too wide: COP's stop was 1.52%, which is tight.
wrong.The flush was too deep: Depth is not the problem. The late reclaim and the sector are.

questions.q: Our research on these bounces found a typical stop of 1.7%. About how big a bounce do you need to reach 3R?
choices: About 5%
About 1.7%
About 9%
About 17%
questions.why: About 5%. One R is your stop distance, so 3R is three of them, and 3 times 1.7% is about 5%. 5R is about 9%. That's why a tight stop is such an edge on these. You don't need a monster bounce to get paid. A normal snapback off a panic low can get you to 3R. The flip side: those marks come fast, so have your selling plan ready before you buy.
questions.lesson_line: Tight stops mean close targets. 3R is about a 5% bounce.

wrong.About 1.7%: That's one R, your stop. 3R is three of them.

questions.simple: About 5%. Three times a 1.7% stop is about 5%, so 3R comes on a normal bounce.

deeper.trap: A big R count can feel like a big move. With a stop this tight, it isn't. 3R is about a 5% bounce and 5R about 9%. ALB shows the extreme: with its tiny stop, 5R was only 3% over the buy.

house: R targets from the rulebook

questions.q: In our scan of 2,220 reclaims, about what share reached 3R before the stop?
choices: About half
About a quarter
About nine in ten
Almost none
questions.why: About half: 52.3% reached 3R and 43.1% reached 5R before the stop. That is a fixed stop with no trims.
questions.lesson_line: About half got to 3R. The stop and trims do the rest.

wrong.About nine in ten: 52.3% reached 3R, and 81% were stopped at some point.

questions.q: In our scan, 52.3% of reclaims hit 3R before the stop, yet 81% got stopped at some point. How can both be true?
choices: Fixed stop, so fades came back
The stop was far too wide
3R is just a bad target here
3R was counted after the stop
questions.answer: Fixed stop, so fades came back
questions.why: The stop never moved. Lots of bounces ran to 3R, then faded all the way back to the original stop. That one trade counts in both numbers. Bounces off a panic low fade, and that's the whole lesson. So you don't sit there with a fixed stop. You sell some into strength and move the stop up to breakeven, somewhere from 2R to 5R. The scan didn't test that plan. It shows you what happens when you do nothing.
questions.lesson_line: Bounces fade. Sell some into strength, then protect the rest.

wrong.3R is just a bad target here: 52.3% got there. The problem is what happened after.
wrong.The stop was far too wide: The stops were tight, a median of about 1.7%.
wrong.3R was counted after the stop: The scan only counts 3R when it came before the stop.

questions.simple: Lots of bounces hit 3R and then faded back to a stop that never moved, so both are true.

deeper.example: Picture a bounce that reaches 3R, then fades. In the scan the stop never moved, so the fade came back and hit it. That trade counts in both numbers. With our plan, some is sold into strength and the stop moves up to breakeven. The same path then keeps a gain.

questions.q: Write the order. What's your entry and stop?

Limit 91.24, stop 87.93

Market 89.37, stop 87.93
questions.story: After a Friday flush, Monday opens at 88.34, under the flush low, and undercuts to 87.93. Then it turns and comes back over the flush low. You buy the reclaim at 89.37.
questions.why: Market at 89.37, stop at 87.88. You buy at market as price comes back through the flush low. A limit order on a turn like this can leave you watching it run without you. The stop goes a few cents under 87.93, the low of the day you bought. A few cents under, not right on it, because a stop sitting on the low gets picked off. That puts it 1.7% from the buy, right inside the 1-3% we like.
questions.lesson_line: Market order on the reclaim. Stop a few cents under the low of the day.

wrong.Limit 91.24, stop 87.93: 91.24 was the close. We buy as price trades through the trigger, never at the close.
wrong.Market 87.93, stop 80.00: 87.93 is the undercut, not the reclaim, and 80.00 is a stop miles away.
wrong.Market 89.37, stop 87.93: A stop right on the low gets picked off. Put it a few cents under.

questions.simple: Buy at market on the reclaim, 89.37, with the stop a few cents under the 87.93 low.

deeper.trap: Two details catch people. The stop goes a few cents under the 87.93 low, not right on it. And the buy is at market as price trades through the trigger, never at the close.

questions.q: What's the trade?
choices: Buy the Monday reclaim of the low
Buy the Friday close of the flush
Buy Monday's open, under the low
Wait two weeks and look again
questions.story: The last bar is a Friday flush. Its low is 23.4% under the 10-day high close, on 2.28 times the usual volume. Monday opens under that low, undercuts it, then climbs back over.
questions.answer: Buy the Monday reclaim of the low
questions.why: Buy the Monday reclaim. Friday's close was the knife, and Monday proved it by opening under the low. Then sellers ran out and buyers took the low back. That reclaim is the trigger, at market, with the stop a few cents under Monday's low. This was OKTA in April 2025: open 88.34, low 87.93, close 91.24. Down days into a Friday, then the turn on a Monday. That's the Monday turn Bracco talks about.
questions.lesson_line: Buy the reclaim of the flush low, not the flush close.

wrong.Buy the Friday close of the flush: That's the knife. Monday opened under it.
wrong.Buy Monday's open, under the low: The open is still under the flush low. Wait till it's back over.
wrong.Wait two weeks and look again: The reclaim is the trigger, and it came Monday. Two weeks later, the trade's gone.

questions.simple: Buy the Monday reclaim. It broke under the flush low, then got back over it, and that's the turn.

deeper.example: OKTA, April 2025: Thursday and Friday flushed it 23%. Monday opened 88.34 under the flush low, undercut to 87.93 and closed 91.24. The reclaim buy was 89.37 with a stop at 87.88, 1.7% away. The Monday is a backdrop. The reclaim is the trigger.

questions.q: The chart ends on a flush day: three lower closes into a round number and the 200-day, on heavy volume. Watch it, or pass?

Pass, a slow grind with no burst
Watch it, buy the next green close
Buy the close, the volume marks the low

Levels like that are where big buyers wait. But today's close isn't the buy. You want the next session to undercut this low and take it back. This one did: it undercut the low the next day and closed 6% higher. That reclaim was the buy.
questions.lesson_line: A fast flush into a real level goes on the watch list.

wrong.Pass, a slow grind with no burst: Look again. Three straight lower closes into a huge bar is a burst, not a grind.
wrong.Watch it, buy the next green close: A green close isn't the trigger. The reclaim of the flush low is.
wrong.Buy the close, the volume marks the low: We never buy the flush close. Nearly half get undercut the next day.

questions.simple: Watch it. It's a fast flush into a real level, and the buy only comes if a later day reclaims the low.

questions.q: A leader dips to its rising 50-day: 2.95 ATR down on 2.23 times volume, 12.9% off its 10-day high close. Watch it, or pass?

Pass, the volume is too light
Watch it, 2.95 ATR is a deep flush
Watch it, a flush into the 50-day

questions.q: Which flush day do you like better?
questions.story: Two stocks flush on 2.3 times their usual volume. For one, that's the biggest volume bar of the whole decline. For the other, an earlier day in the same decline traded more.
choices: The one with no heavier day before
The one with the earlier heavy day
Both read the same, same volume
Neither, it takes 3x to count
questions.answer: The one with no heavier day before
questions.why: The one with no heavier day before it. You want the flush to be the climax, the single heaviest day of the whole drop. That's the day the most holders gave up at once. If an earlier day traded more, the biggest wave of selling already came and went, and this is just another down day. Same 2.3 times on both, but only one is the peak, and that raises the grade. ALGM is the model: seven straight lower closes into a climax bar on the highest volume of the decline.
questions.lesson_line: The best flush bar is the biggest bar of the decline.

wrong.The one with the earlier heavy day: The heaviest selling came earlier, so this flush isn't the climax.
wrong.Both read the same, same volume: Same multiple, but only one is the peak of the selling. That's the one I want.
wrong.Neither, it takes 3x to count: There's no magic multiple. What matters is whether it's the heaviest day of the drop.

questions.simple: The one with no heavier day before. You want the flush to be the heaviest day of the whole drop.

deeper.trap: Heavy volume alone doesn't make a day the climax. You want the heaviest bar of the decline. A flush day beaten by an earlier day is just another down day in the slide.

reasons: the 2x volume is a proposal that may change

questions.q: The best capitulation flushes come on the heaviest volume of the whole decline.
questions.why: True. You want the flush to be the climax, the day the most holders give up at once. If it's also the biggest volume bar of the whole drop, the selling peaked right there. That raises the grade. It's not a must, though. A clean flush on big but not record volume can still work. When you see a flush, look left on the volume bars and ask if anything in the decline beat it.
questions.lesson_line: Biggest volume of the drop on the flush day raises the grade.
questions.simple: True. When the flush is the heaviest day of the drop, the selling peaked right there.

reasons: the 2x gate is the dossier's proposal

questions.q: You want a bounce trade in a $120 stock that averages 400,000 shares a day. What's the most you can own?
questions.why: 4,000 shares. We never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume, and 1% of 400,000 is 4,000. That's a ceiling, whatever your stop would allow. The reason is getting out. On a panic trade the stock can turn on you fast. If you own a big slice of the day's volume, your own selling pushes the price down as you exit. Stay small against the volume and you can always get out clean.
questions.lesson_line: Never own more than 1% of the day's volume.
